claim: Killer meiotic drivers are genetic parasites that destroy 'sibling' gametes lacking the driver allele.
source: Killer meiotic drivers are genetic parasites that destroy 'sibling' gametes lacking the driver allele.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that establishes what killer meiotic drivers are and how they function.

claim: The fitness costs of drive can lead to selection of unlinked suppressors.
source: The fitness costs of drive can lead to selection of unlinked suppressors.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract about evolutionary responses to meiotic drive.

claim: Schizosaccharomyces pombe contains numerous gamete (spore)-killing wtf drivers.
source: Schizosaccharomyces pombe, an organism containing numerous gamete (spore)-killing wtf drivers, offers a tractable system to test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract about S. pombe.

claim: In scenarios analogous to outcrossing, wtf drivers generate a fitness landscape in which atypical spores, such as aneuploids and diploids, are advantageous.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in scenarios analogous to outcrossing, wtf drivers generate a fitness landscape in which atypical spores, such as aneuploids and diploids, are advantageous.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: wtf drivers can decrease the fitness costs of mutations that disrupt meiotic fidelity.
source: In this context, wtf drivers can decrease the fitness costs of mutations that disrupt meiotic fidelity and, in some circumstances, can even make such mutations beneficial.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experiments with various meiotic mutants.

claim: Some S. pombe isolates generate up to 46% aneuploid or diploid spores.
source: Moreover, we find that S. pombe isolates vary greatly in their ability to make haploid spores, with some isolates generating up to 46% aneuploid or diploid spores.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The sickle cell trait provides heterozygous individuals some protection against Plasmodium falciparum.
source: For example, the sickle cell trait has been selected in malaria-endemic human populations as it provides heterozygous individuals some protection against the malaria-causing parasite, Plasmodium falciparum.
evidence: This is cited as an example of evolutionary tradeoffs with references to support it (Elguero et al., 2015; Serjeant, 2010).

claim: Homozygotes for the sickle cell allele develop sickle cell disease.
source: However, the advantages of this allele come with a high cost as homozygotes develop sickle cell disease (Elguero et al., 2015; Serjeant, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Elguero et al., 2015; Serjeant, 2010).

claim: Meiotic drivers are found throughout eukaryotes.
source: Meiotic drivers are one type of selfish DNA element found throughout eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the distribution of meiotic drivers.

claim: Meiotic drive loci can be transmitted to up to 100% of gametes instead of the expected 50%.
source: Rather than being transmitted to 50% of the progeny of a heterozygote, these selfish loci use a variety of tactics to promote their own transmission into up to 100% of the gametes (Sandler and Novitski, 1957; Zimmering et al., 1970).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Sandler and Novitski, 1957; Zimmering et al., 1970).

claim: Different natural S. pombe isolates contain between 4 and 14 predicted wtf drivers.
source: Different natural isolates contain between 4 and 14 predicted wtf drivers, almost all of which are found on chromosome 3 (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).

claim: Almost all wtf drivers are found on chromosome 3.
source: Different natural isolates contain between 4 and 14 predicted wtf drivers, almost all of which are found on chromosome 3 (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).

claim: Each wtf meiotic driver encodes two proteins from two largely overlapping transcripts with distinct start sites: a poison (Wtfpoison) and an antidote (Wtfantidote).
source: Each wtf meiotic driver encodes two proteins from two largely overlapping transcripts with distinct start sites: a poison (Wtfpoison) and an antidote (Wtfantidote) (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claim: In wtf+/wtf- heterozygotes, all developing spores are exposed to Wtfpoison, but only those inheriting wtf+ express the corresponding Wtfantidote.
source: In wtf+/wtf- heterozygotes, all the developing meiotic products (spores) are exposed to the Wtfpoison, but only those that inherit the wtf+ allele express the corresponding Wtfantidote and neutralize the poison.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claim: The poison and antidote proteins of a given wtf meiotic driver share more than 200 amino acid residues.
source: The poison and antidote proteins of a given wtf meiotic driver share a considerable length of amino acid sequence (>200 residues) (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claim: A mismatch of two amino acids within the C-terminus can disrupt the ability of a Wtfantidote to neutralize a Wtfpoison.
source: Strikingly, even a mismatch of two amino acids within the C-terminus can disrupt the ability of a Wtfantidote to neutralize a Wtfpoison (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018).

claim: The antidote of a given wtf gene generally does not neutralize poisons produced by other wtf drivers with distinct sequences.
source: The antidote of a given wtf gene generally does not neutralize poisons produced by other wtf drivers with distinct sequences (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2017).

claim: Heterozygous, competing wtf drivers provide a selective advantage to atypical spores that inherit more than a haploid complement of wtf drivers.
source: Here, we find that heterozygous, competing wtf drivers provide a selective advantage to atypical spores that inherit more than a haploid complement of wtf drivers.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The selective advantage of atypical spores is due to the preferential elimination of haploid spores.
source: This selective advantage is due to the preferential elimination of haploid spores, as these spores are killed by the wtf driver(s) they do not inherit.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: The selected atypical spores include aneuploids, diploids, and spores inheriting wtf gene duplications resulting from unequal crossovers.
source: The selected atypical spores include aneuploids, diploids, and spores inheriting wtf gene duplications resulting from unequal crossovers between homologous chromosomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: Competing wtf drivers generate an environment where variants that disrupt meiotic chromosome segregation can increase fitness.
source: We use a combination of empirical analyses and modeling to demonstrate that competing wtf drivers generate an environment where variants that disrupt meiotic chromosome segregation can increase fitness.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data and modeling.

claim: S. pombe cells generally exist as haploids but will mate to form diploids when starved of nutrients.
source: S. pombe cells generally exist as haploids but will mate to form diploids when starved of nutrients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Egel, 2004; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: When starvation signal is continued, S. pombe diploids will proceed into meiosis resulting in the production of spores.
source: If this starvation signal is continued, these diploids will proceed into meiosis resulting in the production of spores (Egel, 2004; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Egel, 2004; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: All known S. pombe isolates share an average DNA sequence identity of >99% for nonrepetitive regions.
source: All known S. pombe isolates share an average DNA sequence identity of >99% for nonrepetitive regions, and nearly all of these isolates contain three chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about S. pombe isolates.

claim: Nearly all S. pombe isolates contain three chromosomes.
source: All known S. pombe isolates share an average DNA sequence identity of >99% for nonrepetitive regions, and nearly all of these isolates contain three chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about S. pombe isolates.

claim: Outcrossing S. pombe often yields diploids that exhibit low fertility.
source: Despite minimal sequence divergence between the strains, outcrossing often yields diploids that exhibit low fertility (i.e. they produce few viable spores) (Avelar et al., 2013; Gutz and Doe, 1975; Hu et al., 2017; Jeffares et al., 2015; Singh and Klar, 2002; Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Avelar et al., 2013; Gutz and Doe, 1975; Hu et al., 2017; Jeffares et al., 2015; Singh and Klar, 2002; Zanders et al., 2014).

claim: Differences in karyotype between isolates and pervasive meiotic drive are the two demonstrated causes of infertility in heterozygous S. pombe diploids.
source: Differences in karyotype (such as chromosomal rearrangements) between isolates and pervasive meiotic drive are the two demonstrated causes of infertility in heterozygous S. pombe diploids (Avelar et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017; Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Avelar et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017; Zanders et al., 2014).

claim: The majority of surviving spores from Sp/Sk heterozygotes are heterozygous aneuploids or diploids containing both the Sp copy and Sk copy of chromosome 3.
source: Although these Sp/Sk heterozygotes make few viable spores, the majority of the surviving spores are heterozygous aneuploids or diploids, as they contain both the Sp copy and Sk copy of chromosome 3 (Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Zanders et al., 2014).

claim: Disomy of chromosome 3 is the only tolerable aneuploidy within Sp.
source: Disomy of chromosome 3 is the only tolerable aneuploidy within Sp, as spores disomic for chromosomes 1 or 2, or spores lacking any of the three chromosomes are inviable (Niwa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Niwa et al., 2006).

claim: Diploid spores possessing an extra copy of every chromosome are viable.
source: Additionally, diploid spores, or spores possessing an extra copy of every chromosome are viable.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The disomic state of chromosome 3 aneuploids is unstable and the extra chromosome 3 is quickly shed as the spores grow and form colonies.
source: Furthermore, the disomic state of chromosome 3 aneuploids is unstable and the extra chromosome 3 is quickly shed as the spores grow and form colonies (Niwa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Niwa et al., 2006).

claim: Each of the novel heterozygous diploids tested had low viable spore yields compared to homozygous diploid controls.
source: Similar to the previously characterized Sp/Sk heterozygotes, our genetic analyses revealed that each of the novel heterozygous diploids we tested had low viable spore yields compared to homozygous diploid controls (Figure 1B, compare diploids 2–7 to diploids 8–12).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The reduced viable spore yields in heterozygotes are likely due to increased spore death.
source: These reduced yields are likely due to increased spore death in the heterozygotes (Hu et al., 2017; Jeffares et al., 2015; Singh and Klar, 2002; Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on data and supported by citations (Hu et al., 2017; Jeffares et al., 2015; Singh and Klar, 2002; Zanders et al., 2014).

claim: Heterozygous diploids frequently produced spores that grew into small colonies with irregular shapes, a hallmark of aneuploidy.
source: In addition to having low viable spore yields, the heterozygous diploids frequently produced spores that grew into small colonies with irregular shapes, a hallmark of aneuploidy (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Niwa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, with citation (Niwa et al., 2006).

claim: 34–78% of the viable spores produced by heterozygotes were determined to be disomic for chromosome 3.
source: Consistent with this, 34–78% of the viable spores produced by heterozygotes were determined to be disomic for chromosome 3 as they inherited both centromere 3-linked markers (ade6+ and ade6Δ::hphMX6; Figure 1B, diploids 2–7).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The frequency of disomic spores was generally higher in heterozygotes than homozygotes.
source: The frequency of disomic spores was generally higher in heterozygotes than homozygotes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: There was considerable variation amongst the homozygotes with spore disomy frequencies ranging from 5–46%.
source: However, there was considerable variation amongst the homozygotes with spore disomy frequencies ranging from 5–46% (Figure 1B, diploids 8–12).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: In diploids heterozygous for different wtf driving alleles, haploid spores will generally inherit either every Sp driver or every Sk driver.
source: As a result, in diploids heterozygous for different wtf driving alleles, the drivers can be described as 'competing' as they exist on separate haplotypes and produce distinct Wtf proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of wtf drivers.

claim: Heterozygous disomic spores are more likely to inherit all the competing wtf drive alleles.
source: However, heterozygous disomic spores are more likely to inherit all the competing wtf drive alleles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of wtf drivers and chromosome inheritance.

claim: Disomic spores that inherit every wtf driver should survive, as they will contain every Wtfantidote necessary to counteract the Wtf poisons.
source: These disomic spores should thus survive, as they will contain every Wtfantidote necessary to counteract the Wtf poisons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of wtf drivers, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Sp/Sk heterozygotes do not make more disomic spores per meiosis than Sp or Sk homozygotes.
source: Consistent with this model, Sp/Sk heterozygotes do not make more disomic spores per meiosis than Sp or Sk homozygotes (Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Zanders et al., 2014).

claim: 63% of the viable spores generated by the double driver heterozygote appeared to be disomic.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we found that 63% of the viable spores generated by the double driver heterozygote appeared to be disomic as they inherited both alleles at ade6 (ade6-:FY29033 wtf36:natMX4 and ade6-:Sp wtf13:hphMX6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The control diploid (no heterozygous wtf drivers) generated 4% disomic viable spores.
source: This was considerably higher than the control diploid (no heterozygous wtf drivers) in which 4% of the viable spores displayed this phenotype (Figure 2C, compare diploid 13 to 14).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Many of the viable spores produced by the double driver heterozygote generated small, misshapen colonies characteristic of aneuploids.
source: Additionally, many of the viable spores produced by the double driver heterozygote generated small, misshapen colonies characteristic of aneuploids.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by observations.

claim: The fertility of the double driver heterozygote was 20-fold lower than the control diploid.
source: Finally, the fertility of the double driver heterozygote was 20-fold lower than the control diploid (Figure 2C, compare diploid 13 to diploid 14).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Sk wtf28poison/Sk wtf4poison heterozygotes had very low viable spore yields, but did not exhibit a higher frequency of disomic spores than control diploids.
source: We found that Sk wtf28poison/Sk wtf4poison heterozygotes had very low viable spore yields, but did not exhibit a higher frequency of disomic spores than control diploids (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The number of disomic spores produced per cell placed on sporulation media did not increase between the double driver heterozygote and the control diploid.
source: We found that the number of disomic spores produced per cell placed on sporulation media did not increase between the double driver heterozygote and the control diploid (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, compare diploid 13 to diploid 14).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Disomic spores generated from diploids carrying multiple sets of heterozygous wtf meiotic drivers are enriched in the surviving population due to the destruction of haploid spores, rather than due to Wtf proteins increasing the rate of meiotic chromosome missegregation.
source: Together, our results are consistent with our hypothesis that disomic spores generated from diploids carrying multiple sets of heterozygous wtf meiotic drivers are enriched in the surviving population due to the destruction of haploid spores, rather than due to Wtf proteins increasing the rate of meiotic chromosome missegregation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The Sp/Sk mosaic diploid is heterozygous for eight known or predicted wtf meiotic drivers.
source: For these experiments, we started with an Sp/Sk mosaic diploid strain that is heterozygous for eight known or predicted wtf meiotic drivers (Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Eickbush et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental strain with citations (Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Eickbush et al., 2019).

claim: The Sp/Sk mosaic diploid is homozygous for Sk chromosomes 1 and 2 but is heterozygous for most of chromosome 3 for Sp- and Sk-derived sequences.
source: This mosaic diploid is homozygous for Sk chromosomes 1 and 2 but is heterozygous for most of chromosome 3 for Sp- and Sk-derived sequences (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental strain shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The viable spores generated by the rec12Δ Sp/Sk mosaic diploid were almost exclusively (94%) heterozygous disomes for chromosome 3.
source: Consistent with our previous observations in a similar mosaic diploid (Nuckolls et al., 2017), we saw that the viable spores generated by this diploid were almost exclusively (94%) heterozygous disomes for chromosome 3 (Figure 3B, diploid 17).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B with citation (Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claim: rec12Δ Sk homozygous diploids generate only 27% disomic spores.
source: Lack of recombination is, however, insufficient to explain the majority of the phenotype, as rec12Δ Sk homozygous diploids generate only 27% disomic spores (Figure 3B, diploid 19).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Deleting both Sp wtf13 and Sp wtf4 significantly decreased the frequency of chromosome 3 heterozygous disomes from 94% to 67% in the rec12Δ mosaic diploid.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, deleting both Sp drivers significantly decreased the frequency of chromosome 3 heterozygous disomes (from 94% to 67%; Figure 3B, diploids 17 and 18), although it did not significantly increase fertility.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Deleting only one of the two Sp drivers (Sp wtf13 or Sp wtf4) was sufficient to significantly decrease the frequency of disomic spores in the rec12Δ mosaic diploid.
source: Deleting only one of the two Sp drivers was also sufficient to significantly decrease the frequency of disomic spores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, diploids 47 and 48).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deleting only one of the six predicted Sk drivers (wtf4) had no effect on disomy frequency in the rec12Δ mosaic diploid.
source: However, deleting only one of the six predicted Sk drivers (wtf4) had no effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, diploid 49).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rec12+/rec12Δ mosaic diploid had low fertility, similar to that of the rec12Δ Sp/Sk mosaic diploid.
source: We observed that this rec12+/rec12Δ diploid had low fertility, similar to that of the rec12Δ Sp/Sk mosaic diploid (Figure 3B, compare diploid 17 to diploid 20).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: 68% of the viable spores generated by the rec12+/rec12Δ mosaic diploid appeared to be disomic for chromosome 3.
source: We found that 68% of the viable spores generated by this mosaic appeared to be disomic for chromosome 3.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Deleting both Sp wtf4 and Sp wtf13 in the rec12+/rec12Δ mosaic diploid significantly increased fertility and decreased disomy at ade6 amongst the viable spores from 68% to 27%.
source: Deleting both Sp wtf4 and Sp wtf13 in the rec12+/rec12Δ mosaic diploid significantly increased fertility and decreased disomy at ade6 amongst the viable spores from 68% to 27% (Figure 3B, diploids 20 and 21).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: In the Sk double driver heterozygote, the genetic distance between ade6 and ura4 decreased significantly from 75 cM to 44 cM compared to the Sk control.
source: The ade6 and ura4 loci are over 75 cM apart in the Sk control (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). In the Sk double driver heterozygotes, this distance decreased significantly to 44 cM (p-value=0.03, G-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: In the mosaic diploids with all drivers intact, ade6 and ura4 were 43 cM apart.
source: In the mosaic diploids with all drivers intact, we observed ade6 and ura4 were 43 cM apart (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), similar to the 62 cM previously observed in Sp/Sk hybrids (Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with citation (Zanders et al., 2014).

claim: When Sp wtf4 and Sp wtf13 were deleted from the mosaic strain, the observed genetic distance between ade6 and ura4 decreased significantly to 11 cM.
source: However, when Sp wtf4 and Sp wtf13 were deleted from the mosaic strain, the observed genetic distance decreased significantly to 11 cM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; p-value<0.01, G-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Meiotic drivers can directly affect recombination landscapes.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that meiotic drivers can directly affect recombination landscapes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the recombination frequency data.

claim: Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygous diploids had decreased fertility (13% of the control diploid).
source: We found that Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygous diploids had decreased fertility (13% of the control diploid; Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 77% of the viable spores from Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygous diploids appeared to be disomic for chromosome 3.
source: and 77% of the viable spores appeared to be disomic for chromosome 3 as they inherited both Sk wtf4- and Sk wtf28-linked drug resistance markers (G418R HygR spores, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Amongst the G418R HygR spores generated by the Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygote, only 15.4% appeared to be aneuploid and none appeared to be diploid.
source: We were surprised to discover that amongst the G418R HygR spores generated by the Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygote, only 15.4% appeared to be aneuploid and none appeared to be diploid.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The majority (84.6%) of the G418R HygR spores from Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygote appeared to be haploid.
source: Instead, the majority (84.6%) of the G418R HygR spores appeared to be haploid (Figure 4C, diploid 24).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: An unequal interhomolog crossover event at the ade6 locus could lead to duplication of the wtf driver found on the opposite haplotype.
source: We reasoned that an unequal interhomolog crossover event at the ade6 locus could have led to duplication of the wtf driver found on the opposite haplotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The unequal crossover events in Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygote were Rec12-dependent.
source: Consistent with the idea that a crossover placed the competing wtf drivers on one haplotype in the Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 diploid meiosis, the events were Rec12-dependent (Figure 4, diploid 26).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A PCR product consistent with the recombination event was detected in 19 out of the 22 haploid G418R HygR spore colonies tested from Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygote.
source: In addition, we detected a PCR product consistent with the recombination event in 19 out of the 22 haploid G418R HygR spore colonies tested (Figure 4, diploid 24, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Deleting rec12 imposed no fitness cost on Sp/Sk heterozygotes compared to the Sp/Sp or Sk/Sk homozygotes.
source: Consistent with this idea, we previously observed that deleting rec12 imposed no fitness cost on Sp/Sk heterozygotes compared to the Sp/Sp or Sk/Sk homozygotes (Zanders et al., 2014; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Zanders et al., 2014) and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Rec12 did not significantly promote fertility in CBS5680/Sp, JB844/Sp, CBS5680/Sk, and JB844/Sk heterozygotes as it did in homozygotes.
source: We observed that Rec12 did not significantly promote fertility in heterozygotes as it did in homozygotes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: In a diploid with one set of heterozygous drivers (Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 at ade6), the cost of deleting rec12 was similar to that observed in the wild-type background (3-fold decrease in fertility).
source: We found that in a diploid with one set of heterozygous drivers (Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 at ade6), the cost of deleting rec12 (rec12Δ/rec12Δ) was similar to that observed in the wild-type background (3-fold decrease in fertility) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deleting rec12 in a genetic background with wtf drivers competing at both ade6 and ura4 had no cost.
source: However, we found that deleting rec12 in a genetic background with wtf drivers competing at both ade6 and ura4 had no cost (Figure 2C, compare diploid 15 to diploid 13).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Deleting sgo1 and rec10 had a lower fitness cost in the background with heterozygous wtf drivers than in the background without wtf competition (~3 fold decrease compared to a 6–7-fold decrease).
source: Deleting sgo1 and rec10 had a lower fitness cost in the background with heterozygous wtf drivers than in the background without wtf competition (~3 fold decrease compared to a 6–7-fold decrease) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deleting moa1 or rec8 had no effect on fitness in diploids with heterozygous wtf drivers, despite the fact that these mutations decrease fertility by 4- and 6-fold, respectively, in the absence of wtf driver competition.
source: Remarkably, deleting moa1 or rec8 had no effect on fitness in diploids with heterozygous wtf drivers, despite the fact that these mutations decrease fertility by 4- and 6-fold, respectively, in the absence of wtf driver competition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deleting one copy of moa1 did not significantly alter the frequency of disomic spores in the absence of wtf driver competition.
source: Deleting one copy of moa1 did not significantly alter the frequency of disomic spores in the absence of wtf driver competition (Figure 6B, diploid 28).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: Heterozygosity for moa1 did not suppress the fitness costs of wtf competition.
source: In addition, heterozygosity for moa1 did not suppress the fitness costs of wtf competition (Figure 6B, diploid 30).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: Deleting one copy of rec8 significantly increased the production of disomic spores in a background without heterozygous wtf drivers.
source: However, deleting one copy of rec8 significantly increased the production of disomic spores in a background without heterozygous wtf drivers (Figure 6B, diploid 27).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: rec8 exhibits haploinsufficiency and reducing Rec8 protein levels may lead to chromosome segregation errors during meiosis.
source: This suggests that rec8 exhibits haploinsufficiency and reducing Rec8 protein levels may lead to chromosome segregation errors during meiosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data.

claim: rec8 heterozygosity increased the fertility of diploids with competing drivers.
source: As hypothesized, rec8 heterozygosity also increased the fertility of diploids with competing drivers (Figure 6B, diploid 29).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: The higher the strength of drive (t), the lower the number of drivers required for mutant invasion.
source: Interestingly, the higher the strength of drive (t), the lower the number of drivers required for mutant invasion (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the population genetic modeling shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Drive strength is generally high (t >0.9) in S. pombe.
source: Importantly, our empirical work demonstrates that drive strength is generally high (t >0.9) and that there are ample distinct wtf driver haplotypes (Eickbush et al., 2019) leaving parameter space for mutants to invade even if they incur considerable costs (sm and ss) (Appendix 1—figure 1; Bravo Núñez et al., 2018; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from empirical work with citations (Eickbush et al., 2019; Bravo Núñez et al., 2018; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claim: There are ample distinct wtf driver haplotypes in S. pombe.
